questions.stem: Within which band must the fundamental frequency of a 150 m vessel's whistle lie?
questions.explanation: Annex III sets 130-350 Hz for vessels of 75 m but less than 200 m. 70-200 Hz is for 200 m or more and 250-700 Hz for under 75 m. All fundamentals lie within 70-700 Hz, so nothing above 700 Hz is a fundamental band.

questions.stem: Which frequency band carries the range of the whistle on an 18 m vessel under the international text of Annex III, and how does the Canadian modification treat a roadstead, harbour, river, lake or inland waterway?
options: 180-700 Hz; Canada makes no change for its inland waters
180-2 100 Hz; upper limit may extend to 2 100 Hz there
70-200 Hz; in those Canadian waters it may drop to 50 Hz
250-700 Hz only; Canada forbids frequencies above 700 Hz
questions.explanation: The range-determining band is 180-700 Hz for vessels of 20 m or more and 180-2 100 Hz for vessels under 20 m. The Canadian modification allows the upper limit to be extended to 2 100 Hz in Canadian waters of a roadstead, harbour, river, lake or inland waterway. 250-700 Hz is the fundamental band for vessels under 75 m, a different requirement.

questions.stem: Annex III gives a typical audibility range for the whistle of a 40 m vessel. What is it, and what is its status under the Canadian Regulations?
options: 2 miles; a legal minimum in Canada
1 mile; for information only
0.5 mile; a legal minimum everywhere
1.5 miles; fog only
questions.explanation: The table gives 1 mile for vessels of 20 m to under 75 m (2 miles for 200 m or more, 1.5 for 75-200 m, 0.5 for under 20 m). The Canadian Annex III states that the audibility-range column and its notes are not part of the Regulations, and Annex III itself says real range varies widely with wind and noise.

questions.stem: A vessel's only whistle is directional. What must be true of its sound abeam compared with ahead?
options: It may be silent abeam, as long as it is loud ahead
Within 10 dB of on-axis, so abeam range is half or more
It must be exactly as loud abeam as it is ahead
It must be no more than 4 dB below the on-axis level in every direction
questions.explanation: Within 45 degrees of the axis a directional whistle may be no more than 4 dB below the prescribed level; in any other horizontal direction (such as abeam) no more than 10 dB below, so its range in any direction is at least half its forward range. As the only whistle it must point straight ahead.

questions.stem: Your lookout on the bridge wing complains that your own whistle is deafening. Which Annex III requirement applies?
options: The whistle should be mounted as low as possible to keep it away from the bridge
Max 110 dB(A) at listening posts, 100 if practicable
No limit: louder is safer
The whistle must be switched off whenever a lookout is posted
questions.explanation: Annex III places the whistle as high as practicable, partly to protect the crew's hearing, and limits the vessel's own signal at the listening posts to 110 dB(A), and so far as practicable 100 dB(A). The Canadian text defines listening posts as the bridge wings or the bow.

questions.stem: A ship has one whistle forward and one aft, 150 m apart. Which statement is correct?
options: They must sound together
Never sounded together; a combined system needs 100 m max
Whistles more than 100 m apart count as a combined whistle system
Any two whistles on one vessel must differ in frequency by at least 100 Hz
questions.explanation: Whistles fitted more than 100 m apart must not be sounded simultaneously. A combined whistle system has whistles no more than 100 m apart, sounded together, differing by at least 10 Hz, and is treated as a single whistle. Rule 34 also says only one of two widely spaced whistles is used for manoeuvring and warning signals.

questions.stem: You are fitting a bell to a 25 m vessel. Which specification meets Annex III?
options: Mouth at least 200 mm, any material, striker at least 1 per cent of the bell's mass
300 mm+, corrosion-proof, 110 dB at 1 m, 3% striker, manual
Mouth at least 300 mm, power striker only, no manual operation needed
Mouth at least 500 mm, giving at least 143 dB at 1 m
questions.explanation: A bell or gong must give at least 110 dB at 1 m, be corrosion-resistant with a clear tone, and on a vessel of 20 m or more have a mouth of at least 300 mm. The striker weighs at least 3 per cent of the bell. A power striker is recommended, but manual operation must remain possible. 143 dB is the whistle figure for vessels of 200 m or more.

questions.stem: Which statement about sound signal gear for small vessels is correct, and who approves the gear on a Canadian vessel?
options: A 17 m vessel needs a 300 mm bell; approval is by the vessel's insurer
An 11 m pleasure boat needs a whistle meeting the 20-75 m figures; approval is by the builder
17 m: no bell, 0.5 mile whistle; 11 m: other sound means; Minister approves
Vessels under 20 m are exempt from all of Rule 33 and Annex III
questions.explanation: Rule 33 requires a bell only from 20 m, so the 300 mm bell size does not apply to a 17 m vessel, and Annex III gives about 0.5 mile as the typical whistle range under 20 m. Under 12 m no whistle or bell is required, but some other efficient means of sound signalling is. The appropriate Canadian authority for sound signal appliances is the Minister.
